newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Guinea-Bissau swaps to CFA franc on August 1.
newsitem.headline: Guinea-Bissau swaps to CFA franc on August 1.

text.p: Guinea-Bissau, an impoverished, Portuguese-speaking West African country of one million people, becomes a fully-fledged member of the Franc Zone when it swaps its present currency, the peso, for the CFA franc on August 1.

Guinea-Bissau joined the West African Monetary Union (UMOA) alongside Benin, Burkina Faso, Ivory Coast, Mali, Niger, Senegal and Togo in May. The central bank of this West African part of the zone, the BCEAO, is in Dakar, Senegal.
The BCEAO official in charge of the swap said it would be completed on time, despite rumours to the contrary.

"To cut short this rumour, I had to go on television (in Guinea-Bissau) last Thursday to say that the operation is finishing on July 31, no later," Patrice Kouame told Ivory Coast daily Fraternite-Matin in an interview.

The authorities had given themselves three months because of the geographical difficulties of effecting the change in a country of many islands and villages, he said. Pesos and CFA francs have been circulating in tandem during this period.
"Given the communications problems between the villages, we had to mobilise a helicopter for a week to carry out exchange operations on the various inhabited islands," Kouame said.
The pesos are being swapped at a rate of 65 per one CFA franc, a figure he acknowledged might cause problems of arithmetic for poorly-educated peasants and other citizens.
However, that was the market rate prevailing in December when the decision to bring in Guinea-Bissau was taken, he said. The peso had fallen from 42 per CFA franc at the end of 1995.
The CFA franc itself is fixed at 100 per French Franc, and there are currently around 620 CFA francs per U.S. dollar.
Kouame denied the currency change had fuelled inflation in Guinea-Bissau, although he said some traders might have taken advantage of the situation to round up, or simply push up, prices.
The authorities had monitored a basket of 26 prices and, while some had risen, that was mainly due to seasonal factors.

Rice had gone up, for example, because at this time of the year traders use it to pay farmers for their cashew nut crop. Since it is being used as a currency as well as a foodstuff, demand is high and the price traditionally rises.

Kouame sidestepped a question on whether neighbouring Guinea might join the Zone. BCEAO governor Charles Konan Banny said recently it would be a good thing if Guinea and Gambia, a state almost entirely enclosed by Senegal, were members.

The present members are in the process of creating a free trade zone and deepening the union in other ways to transform it into the West African Economic and Monetary Union (UEMOA). -- Alan Raybould, Abidjan newsroom +225 21 90 90
